workflow.round_rule: Every round adds or updates exactly one task: set attempts += 1, last_attempt = today, refresh status, and append to evidence. objectives.json is regenerated at the end of the round.
workflow.maths_rule: Do the mathematics in Python first, test the script (it must run and its output must be reproducible), then state and prove the corresponding Lean theorem. A task is done only when both the Python and the Lean exist, or when the task is purely mathematical/numerical.
workflow.formalisation_rule: No sorry, no admit, no axiom, no native_decide. Every declaration's #print axioms must be [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]; footprints are tracked in lean/Axioms*.lean.
workflow.dependency_rule: The Lean module graph and every task's theorem -> module link live in this file under lean_dependencies and tasks[].lean.

tractability.1: out of reach — no known method
tractability.2: low — needs a new idea, a large computation, or substantial formalisation
tractability.3: medium — a focused round; bounded mathematics or formalisation
tractability.4: high — mechanical or nearly so once the statement is right
tractability.5: routine — a script or a one-line proof

value.3: closes a sub-question or a verification gap
value.4: closes a stated objective or unblocks a route
value.5: a new theorem, or a negative result that redirects the programme

objectives.title: Can Routes A, B, C be generalised?
objectives.reason_to_exist: The three certification routes of round 010 were built for the Riemann zeta function: Route A (a sign change plus a one-signed derivative pins one simple on-line zero), Route B (a rigorous count plus matching certificates closes a whole window), Route C (a validated error budget for the explicit formula). Each is a *method*, so the question 'does it generalise?' decides whether the programme's certification machinery is a zeta-specific trick or a reusable instrument. The audit answer is layered and worth recording: the theorem cores are already general in Lean (stated for an arbitrary continuous f : R -> R, an arbitrary Finset, an arbitrary f : C -> C with a functional equation, conjugation reality and analyticity); what is not general is the per-object instantiation -- an interval evaluator, a functional equation, reality, an explicit formula. Instantiating on the Dirichlet L-function reduces the whole question to one substantive Mathlib gap.

tasks.goal: Sharp archimedean rate: ‖Γ(σ+it)‖ ≤ C(1+|t|)^(σ−1/2) exp(−(π/2)|t|) on Re ∈ [1/4,1].
tasks.approach: ROUND 53 -- HAZARD RELAXED BY THE USER: complex Stirling is now AUTHORISED.  With it, T6 is unblocked and its route is refined by measurement (journal 319, probe gammaseq_rate_probe.py).  Two regimes must be separated.  (A) n ~ |t|: replacing n! by Stirling and keeping the product crude caps the rate at 1 + (1/2)(log 2 - 2 + pi/2) = 1.131972, which IDENTIFIES the 0.132 constant journal 266 measured as that closed form -- so Stirling on n! alone does NOT reach pi/2 = 1.570796.  (B) n -> infinity with |t| fixed: here pi/2 lives, and it is an ARGUMENT effect, coming from Re(s log s) = sigma log|s| - |t| arg(s) with arg(s) -> pi/2; the exact |Gamma| rate divided by pi/2 measures 0.995, 1.001, 1.001 at t = 20, 100, 400.  So the route is the n -> infinity LIMIT of the product sum, i.e. Euler-Maclaurin-type real analysis on sum_{k<=n} log|s+k| -- not Stirling alone.  Mathlib supplies Stirling for n! (Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Stirling.lean: factorial_isEquivalent_stirling, le_factorial_stirling, sqrt_pi_le_stirlingSeq) but nothing for that limit, so the limit is the new work, opened as O1.T12.  Route A (GammaSeq, the project's Stirling-free path): the probe shows the committed bound ‖GammaSeq‖ ≤ (1/σ)⌈|t|⌉!/|t|^⌈|t|⌉ delivers exponent rate → 1, while the true rate is π/2 ≈ 1.5708; the discarded product mass Σ_j log√((σ+j)²+t²) − (n+1)log|t| is only ≈ 0.132·|t|, so the diagonal rate of GammaSeq is 1.132 — still short. Because norm_GammaSeq_le_eventually is uniform in n ≥ ⌈|t|⌉, ANY such bound is capped at rate 1; the sharp rate lives in the limit n → ∞ at fixed t, i.e. it IS Stirling. Route A is therefore CLOSED (refuted sub-route, measured). Route B (reflection, 1/Γ(σ+it) = ‖sin(πσ)‖·‖Γ(1−σ−it)‖/π) reduces to the same target.

tasks.blocked_reason: THREE consecutive rounds on the same condition, so per policy this task is reported blocked rather than pursued further.  The condition: the sharp rate exp(-(pi/2)|t|) with (1+|t|)^(sigma-1/2) is STIRLING-strength, and every route the project is allowed to take is shut.  (1) The GammaSeq route is capped at rate 1 (journal 266): any bound uniform in n >= ceil|t| cannot reach pi/2.  (2) The REFLECTION route is confirmed closed by measurement (journals 316-317): Gamma(s)Gamma(1-s) = pi/sin(pi s) is exact, and while the 1/|sin| factor supplies rate pi (STRONGER than pi/2, so the exponential rate is not the obstruction), the identity needs a LOWER bound on |Gamma(1-sigma-it)|, and that factor itself carries exactly the Stirling decay e^{-pi|t|/2} -- so reflection relocates Stirling rather than avoiding it.  (3) The hazards EXCLUDE complex Stirling, which is precisely what (1) and (2) leave as the only remaining tool.  So T6 cannot be advanced without renegotiating the no-complex-Stirling hazard, which is a user-level decision, not a formalisation step.

tasks.decision: The interface must be RESTATED before anything can be discharged from it. strip_edge_divergence_probe.py shows the horizontal-edge integral int_{1/2}^{1} ||logDeriv (x + i*t0)|| dx diverges whenever t0 is the ordinate of a zero of the completed L-function with Re in [1/2,1]: at the critical-line zero gamma_1 it grows exactly like log(1/2eps) (measured offset -0.19497, stable to 5 digits from eps=1e-4 to 1e-8), while at a generic height it converges to 0.4823. Consequence: the objective 'discharge CriticalStripLogDerivBound' is ill-posed as stated. tasks.goal: Restate the interface so its contour avoids zeros.
tasks.approach: Two candidate restatements, both preserving the interface's *use* (bounding the contour integral by C(1+log(NT))(1+|t1-t0|)) while making it well-posed: (i) perturb the horizontal edges to Im = t0 + delta and Im = t1 - delta for a fixed delta > 0, so the segment's distance to every zero is >= delta (needs the explicit zero-avoidance statement); or (ii) quantify only over (t0,t1) in the complement of the (countable, discrete) set of zero ordinates, carrying that hypothesis as 'the horizontal edges are zero-free'.  Option (i) is more symmetric and is what the classical arguments do; option (ii) is closer to the current text.  Either way the consumer dirichletCompleted_zeroCount_le_of_criticalStrip must be re-derived, and the change must NOT weaken the interface (the goal forbids that): the restatement must still imply the same count bound.

tasks.goal: hH's integrable case: a uniform horizontal-edge bound.
tasks.approach: [ROUND 42 PLAN, with the exact lemmas identified] The route for hH is the total-variation split of log Lambda along the horizontal segment: int ||Lambda'/Lambda|| <= Var(log|Lambda|) + Var(arg Lambda).  Concretely the pieces are: (a) UPPER bound on |Lambda| on the strip -- available, journal 225; (b) LOWER bound on |Lambda| on the segment UNIFORM in t -- Mathlib supplies the needed quantitative zero-free input as DirichletCharacter.norm_LFunction_product_ge_one (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/Nonvanishing.lean:310), which combined with the two horizontal isBigO lemmas in the same file gives ||L(1+x+iy)|| >= c x^{3/4} UNIFORMLY in y (journal 278); (c) the ARG variation -- this is the step to watch, because hH feeds the zero count, so the arg bound must NOT come from the count.  BEFORE writing anything, resolve two API questions: does the tree or Mathlib have a Variation-style split for a path integral of logDeriv (candidates: anything named variation / eVariation / totalVariation / length), and can Var(arg Lambda) along a HORIZONTAL segment be bounded from the strip bounds alone.  Also useful and cheap: in the ZERO-FREE case the Integrable hypothesis of hH is automatic from the tree's continuousOn_logDeriv_dirichletCompleted (DirichletAnalytic.lean:87) via ContinuousOn.integrableOn_Icc plus restriction from Ioc 0 1 to Ioc (1/2) 1 -- so hH's only real content is the quantitative uniformity, not integrability.  The LAST remaining input to the interface.  After journal 302 the exceptional heights cost nothing, so hH reduces to: for |t| <= T and the horizontal integrand Integrable on [1/2,1], the integral of ||Lambda'/Lambda(sigma + i t)|| over sigma in [1/2,1] is at most C (1 + log(N(T+2))) UNIFORMLY in t.  Uniformity is the crux: compactness plus the tree's continuity lemma gives only a t-dependent sup (journal 301).  Journal 117 warns that a pointwise bound is NOT the route -- ||Lambda'/Lambda|| is unbounded near a zero even where defined -- so the route is: write log Lambda = log|Lambda| + i arg Lambda along the segment and bound the integral by the total variation of log|Lambda| plus that of arg Lambda.  The first needs an upper bound on |Lambda| on the strip (journal 225, available) and a LOWER bound on |Lambda| on the segment, uniform in t -- which is exactly what Mathlib's quantitative zero-free bound norm_LFunction_product_ge_one (journal 278) supplies in the form |L(1+x+iy)| >= c x^{3/4} uniformly in y.  The second (arg variation) is where the argument principle would enter, and it is the step to watch for circularity: hH feeds the count, so the arg bound must NOT come from the count.  Unknowns to resolve first: whether the tree has a Variation-style split, and whether the arg variation can be bounded directly from the strip bounds.

objectives.title: Decomposition-lab §2–§3 and the zeta series: what the harmonic tier can and cannot do
objectives.reason_to_exist: decomposition_lab.html §2–§3 proposes a greedy Egyptian decomposition of integers and rationals, promoted to 1/2, as a way to *decompose the terms of ζ into a second-tier harmonic series*. If that worked it would be a term-level handle on ζ(s) = Σ n^(−s) and hence on the location of zeros. The note settles it: the operation is a representation-theoretic identity whose only invariant is the *sum* of the represented numbers, so applying it to the indices produces ≥ e^(n−γ) terms; and no partition of the terms into positive/negative Re, Im or vectors can locate a zero, because the zero lives in the Euler–Maclaurin tail, not in the terms. Recording the verdict prevents the lab's idea from being re-attempted as if open.

objectives.title: The η/Euler route to ζ on the critical line: alternation, the odd/even split, and convergence acceleration
objectives.reason_to_exist: η(s) = (1 − 2^{1−s})ζ(s) converges for Re s > 0, so on the critical line one can evaluate ζ from an alternating series and, via Euler's transformation, from a geometrically weighted one. The odd/even split isolates the two sums whose growing parts must cancel, and the accelerator family (Euler, Aitken Δ², Shanks, Wynn ε) is the natural toolkit. The objective is to decide how far this gets: a fast evaluator, or a certification route? The verdict is that it is an evaluator — the raw partial sum at a zero is not zero, and the difference table shows why — which is exactly the distinction the programme's Routes A/B/C were built to supply.

tasks.goal: Show why the growing parts cancel (Euler–Maclaurin).
tasks.approach: Apply Euler–Maclaurin to each parity class; the divergent parts are equal and opposite.
